sb-01.lessons.0.blocks.0.html: A database is an organised store of data. The data lives in tables: columns define the structure (name, type), rows hold the data itself. This is the foundation of the Data Engineer profession.
sb-01.lessons.0.blocks.1.html: SQL is the query language for a database. T-SQL is the SQL dialect of Microsoft SQL Server, and it is exactly what the mentor's programme requires (Week 1: install SQL Server 2019 + SSMS).
sb-01.lessons.0.blocks.2.html: This site has a real SQL engine built in — every query runs right in the browser against a training electronics-shop database. The syntax of the basic queries is the same in the trainer and in SQL Server; where they differ I mark it with an “in SQL Server” note.
sb-01.lessons.0.title: What a database and SQL are
sb-01.lessons.1.blocks.1.html:
• customers — customers (id, name, city, country, reg_date)
  • products — products (id, name, category_id, price, stock)
  • categories — product categories
  • orders — orders (id, customer_id, order_date, status)
  • order_items — order contents (order_id, product_id, qty, unit_price)
  • employees — employees (id, name, title, manager_id, salary, city)
sb-01.lessons.1.blocks.2.html: Take a look at the customers — run the query:
sb-01.lessons.1.blocks.4.html: SELECT * FROM table means “select every column from the table”. The asterisk = all columns.
sb-01.lessons.1.title: Our practice database: a store
sb-01.lessons.2.blocks.0.html: In real work you almost never pull every column — you list the ones you need, separated by commas:
sb-01.lessons.2.blocks.2.html: A column can be given an alias with AS — that is how reports are made readable:
sb-01.lessons.2.blocks.4.html: SQL is case-insensitive (select = SELECT), but keywords are conventionally written in CAPITALS. A query ends with a semicolon.
sb-01.lessons.2.title: SELECT: choosing columns
sb-01.lessons.3.blocks.0.html: Tables are created with CREATE TABLE — each column gets a type. The main types in SQL Server:
sb-01.lessons.3.blocks.1.html:
• INT — whole numbers
  • DECIMAL(10,2) — exact decimals (money!)
  • NVARCHAR(100) — text up to 100 characters (N = unicode)
  • DATE, DATETIME2 — dates
  • BIT — yes/no
sb-01.lessons.3.blocks.3.html: In the trainer (SQLite) the types are simpler: INTEGER, REAL, TEXT, and instead of IDENTITY the auto-number comes from INTEGER PRIMARY KEY. The idea is the same.
sb-01.lessons.3.title: CREATE TABLE and data types
sb-01.lessons.4.blocks.0.html: Constraints protect the data from rubbish — they come up in every interview:
sb-01.lessons.4.blocks.1.html:
• PRIMARY KEY — the unique identifier of a row
  • FOREIGN KEY — a reference to a row in another table (this is how products.category_id → categories.id are linked)
  • NOT NULL — the column must have a value
  • UNIQUE — values do not repeat
  • DEFAULT — a default value
  • CHECK — your own rule (for example, the price must be above zero)
sb-01.lessons.4.blocks.3.html: This is exactly what the mentor's HW Week 1 asks for: HR and Store databases with CHECK, DEFAULT and foreign keys. After this module the homework will make sense.
sb-01.lessons.4.title: Constraints · Week 1
sb-01.quiz.0.explain: SELECT * selects all columns; with no condition every row comes back.
sb-01.quiz.0.options.1: Selects every column and row from orders
sb-01.quiz.1.explain: DECIMAL stores exact decimal values — for money you must not use the approximate FLOAT.
sb-01.quiz.1.q: Which SQL Server type is right for storing money?
sb-01.quiz.2.explain: A primary key uniquely identifies every row — usually the id column.
sb-01.quiz.2.options.1: The unique identifier of a row
sb-01.quiz.2.options.2: The first column of a table
sb-01.quiz.3.explain: A foreign key points at a row in another table: orders.customer_id → customers.id.
sb-01.quiz.3.options.1: To link to a row in another table
sb-01.quiz.3.q: What is a FOREIGN KEY for?
sb-01.quiz.4.explain: CHECK defines an arbitrary rule for a column's values.
sb-01.quiz.4.q: Which constraint forbids storing a negative price?
sb-01.quiz.5.explain: IDENTITY(start, step) is auto-increment. HW Week 1 needs IDENTITY(100,10)!
sb-01.quiz.5.q: What does IDENTITY(1,1) do in SQL Server?
sb-01.tagline: What a database is, tables and first queries · Week 1

sb-02.lessons.0.blocks.0.html: WHERE keeps only the rows where the condition is true. The operators: =, <> (not equal), >, <, >=, <=:
sb-02.lessons.0.blocks.2.html: Text is compared in single quotes. Conditions are joined with AND / OR, just like in Python:
sb-02.lessons.0.title: WHERE — the row filter
sb-02.lessons.1.blocks.1.html:
• IN (a, b, c) — the value is in the list
  • BETWEEN x AND y — a range, bounds included
  • LIKE — a text pattern: % — any characters, _ — exactly one character
sb-02.lessons.1.title: IN, BETWEEN, LIKE
sb-02.lessons.2.blocks.0.html: NULL means “no data”. Ordinary comparisons do not work with it: manager_id = NULL will NOT work. Only IS NULL / IS NOT NULL:
sb-02.lessons.2.blocks.2.html: The director has no manager — hence NULL. This is an interview classic: “why does = NULL not work?” The answer: NULL is not even equal to itself, and any comparison with NULL yields “unknown”.
sb-02.lessons.2.title: NULL — the absence of a value
sb-02.lessons.3.blocks.0.html: ORDER BY sorts the result: ASC — ascending (the default), DESC — descending. DISTINCT removes duplicates:
sb-02.lessons.3.blocks.3.html: Limiting the number of rows: in SQL Server it is SELECT TOP 3 …, in the trainer (SQLite) and PostgreSQL it is LIMIT 3 at the end of the query:
sb-02.lessons.3.title: ORDER BY and DISTINCT
sb-02.lessons.4.blocks.0.html: CASE is if/elif/else inside SQL. It creates a computed column:
sb-02.lessons.4.blocks.2.html: The order of branches matters — the first matching one wins, like elif in Python. CASE is used constantly in reports and data marts.
sb-02.lessons.4.title: CASE — conditions inside a query
sb-02.quiz.0.explain: Filtering rows is what WHERE condition does.
sb-02.quiz.0.q: How do you select products cheaper than 100?
sb-02.quiz.1.explain: <> means “not equal” (in most database systems != also works).
sb-02.quiz.2.explain: Only IS NULL and IS NOT NULL work with NULL — comparing with = always yields “unknown”.
sb-02.quiz.2.q: How do you find rows where manager_id is empty?
sb-02.quiz.3.explain: % matches any continuation, so the pattern “А%” means starts with А.
sb-02.quiz.3.options.3: Names consisting of exactly one letter А
sb-02.quiz.4.explain: DESC means descending. Without it, sorting is ascending (ASC).
sb-02.quiz.4.q: How do you sort by price from expensive to cheap?
sb-02.quiz.5.explain: It is the same row limit, just different dialects: SELECT TOP 5 (T-SQL) versus LIMIT 5.
sb-02.quiz.5.options.0: It does not — TOP is SQL Server, LIMIT is SQLite/PostgreSQL
sb-02.quiz.5.q: How does TOP differ from LIMIT?
sb-02.quiz.6.explain: Like else in Python: nothing matched, so ELSE is taken (without ELSE it would be NULL).
sb-02.quiz.6.q: What does CASE return if no WHEN matched and there is an ELSE?
sb-02.tagline: WHERE, ORDER BY, DISTINCT, NULL, CASE · Week 2

sb-03.lessons.0.blocks.0.html: SQL can process text right inside a query. The main functions (T-SQL → trainer):
sb-03.lessons.0.blocks.1.html:
• UPPER / LOWER — case (the same everywhere)
  • LEN → LENGTH — string length
  • SUBSTRING → SUBSTR — part of a string
  • Concatenation: + or CONCAT in T-SQL, || in the trainer
  • REPLACE — replacement (the same)
sb-03.lessons.0.title: String functions
sb-03.lessons.1.blocks.0.html: ROUND(x, n) rounds to n decimals. Parts can be extracted from a date: in T-SQL — YEAR(d), MONTH(d), DATEDIFF, DATEADD, GETDATE(); in the trainer — strftime:
sb-03.lessons.1.blocks.3.html: In the mentor's Week 2 programme three videos are devoted to datetime functions — an important topic for a Data Engineer (date partitions, monthly reports).
sb-03.lessons.1.title: Numbers and dates
sb-03.lessons.2.blocks.0.html: CAST(x AS type) converts a type — like int() and str() in Python:
sb-03.lessons.2.blocks.2.html: COALESCE(a, b, …) returns the first non-NULL value — the main way to replace emptiness with a default:
sb-03.lessons.2.blocks.4.html: T-SQL also has ISNULL(a, b) — the same thing but for two arguments only. Interviewers love asking about the difference.
sb-03.lessons.2.title: CAST and COALESCE
sb-03.lessons.3.blocks.0.html: The results of two queries can be combined like sets:
sb-03.lessons.3.blocks.1.html:
• UNION — a union without duplicates
  • UNION ALL — a union keeping duplicates (faster)
  • EXCEPT — rows of the first query that are absent from the second
  • INTERSECT — only the shared rows
sb-03.lessons.3.blocks.3.html: The rule: the number and types of columns must match in both queries. These are the Week 2 video topics: Union, Except, Intersect.
sb-03.lessons.3.title: UNION, EXCEPT, INTERSECT
sb-03.quiz.0.explain: In SQLite/PostgreSQL concatenation is ||. In T-SQL it is + or CONCAT.
sb-03.quiz.0.q: How do you concatenate strings in the trainer (SQLite)?
sb-03.quiz.1.explain: COALESCE goes left to right and returns the first non-NULL — that is 5.
sb-03.quiz.2.explain: UNION de-duplicates (slower), UNION ALL simply stacks the results.
sb-03.quiz.2.options.1: UNION removes duplicates, UNION ALL does not
sb-03.quiz.2.options.3: UNION works with a single table
sb-03.quiz.2.q: How does UNION differ from UNION ALL?
sb-03.quiz.3.explain: EXCEPT is set difference: “what I have and you do not”.
sb-03.quiz.3.options.1: Rows of the first query that are absent from the second
sb-03.quiz.4.explain: CAST(value AS type) is the SQL standard. T-SQL also has CONVERT.
sb-03.quiz.4.q: How do you convert price to an integer?
sb-03.quiz.5.explain: In SQL Server it is LEN(), in SQLite/PostgreSQL LENGTH(). Different dialects!
sb-03.tagline: Strings, dates, CAST, UNION and EXCEPT · Week 2
